PQ31.brief: A container is a variable that holds many values instead of one. Unreal has three kinds: an Array is an ordered list where each item has a number called its index, a Set is a group where every item must be different, and a Map stores pairs made of a key and a value, so you can look up a value by its key. Almost every gameplay system stores lists of things, so you will use these all the time. In this quest you make one of each and print what is inside them.
checklist: Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_Containers. Add a String variable named Names. Click the Variable Type icon next to the type and pick the Array container, so the variable holds a list of Strings.
Click Compile. Then open Class Defaults and add 4 default items to Names (for example Apple, Banana, Cherry, Date).
Add a second String variable and turn it into a Set (the { } option in the same container menu). Try to add the same item twice and read the warning that appears.
Add a Map variable with a String key and an Integer value, and name it Scores. Add 3 key-value pairs in the defaults.
On Event BeginPlay, add a For Each Loop node that goes through Names. Use Print String to print each item together with its index.
Use the Find node on Scores with one key, and print the value it returns. Then use Contains Item on the Set and print the result.
Press Play. Read the Output Log and check the order of the printed items and their index numbers.
PQ31.done_when: Send one screenshot of the My Blueprint panel that shows the three container variables (Array, Set, Map) with their type icons, and one screenshot of the Output Log with the printed items and index numbers.

PQ32.brief: A reference to an Actor is often general: Unreal only knows that it is some Actor. A Cast To node asks if that Actor is really a more specific Blueprint class. If it is, you can use the functions of that class. If it is not, the cast fails and the Cast Failed pin runs instead. In this quest you make the player character cast the Actors it touches, and you see both the success and the failure.
checklist: In a Third Person project, make a Blueprint named BP_RotateActor with a Static Mesh that uses Shape_Cube. On Event Tick, call AddActorLocalRotation with Z = 2.0, and put it behind a Branch node that reads a Boolean variable named CanRotate.
Add a function named OverlappedPlayer with a Boolean input named Begin Overlap. Inside the function, use that input to set CanRotate.
Open the ThirdPersonCharacter Blueprint and add a Sphere Collision component with Radius 200. Add the events OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentEndOverlap for it.
Drag from the Other Actor pin and add a Cast To BP_RotateActor node. From the As BP Rotate Actor pin, call OverlappedPlayer. Pass True on the begin overlap event and False on the end overlap event.
Connect a Print String node to the Cast Failed pin, so you can see when the cast does not work. Place BP_RotateActor and one plain cube in the level.
Press Play and walk near both objects. The cube from BP_RotateActor should spin, and the plain cube should print the failed message.
PQ32.done_when: Send a screenshot of the character graph that shows the Cast To node with the Cast Failed pin in use, and a screenshot in Play mode with the actor spinning near the player.

PQ33.brief: A variable can point to one real object that exists in the level, or it can point to a class, which is the recipe used to create new objects. The first is called an Object Reference and the second a Class Reference. They have different icons and pin colors, and mixing them up is a common mistake. In this quest you use an Object Reference to switch one placed lamp on and off, and a Class Reference to spawn new lamps.
checklist: Open a Third Person project that has Starter Content. Place Blueprint_CeilingLight in the level.

In the ThirdPersonCharacter Blueprint, add a variable named LampReference. Set its type to Blueprint Ceiling Light and choose Object Reference. Enable Instance Editable, which lets you set the value on the character placed in the level.
Add an event for the F key. Use a Flip Flop node and Set Visibility to turn the lamp's Point Light 1 on and off through LampReference.
Select the character in the level. In the Details panel, open the Lamp Reference dropdown and pick the lamp you placed. Press Play and press F.
Add a second variable named LampClass. Set its type to Blueprint Ceiling Light and choose Class Reference. Set its default value to Blueprint_CeilingLight.
Add an event for the G key. Use Spawn Actor from Class with LampClass, and spawn the lamp at the player location plus 200 units forward.
Compare the icons of the two variables and the colors of their pins. Write one sentence that says what each variable holds.
PQ33.done_when: Send a screenshot of the graph that shows both variables in use (one Object Reference and one Class Reference). Add one sentence that explains the difference in your own words.

PQ34.brief: A Blueprint Interface is a list of function names with no code inside. Any Blueprint can add the interface and then give its own answer to those functions. This lets very different Actors, such as a lamp and a door, respond to the same call, and the caller does not need to know which kind of Actor it is talking to. In this quest you make one Interact interface, add it to two Actors, and call it from the player character.
checklist: Create a Blueprint Interface named BPI_Interact with one function named Interact. Click Compile and save it.
Duplicate Blueprint_CeilingLight and name the copy BP_Lamp. Add a custom event named ToggleLight that uses Flip Flop and Set Visibility on Point Light 1 to turn the light on and off.
In BP_Lamp, open Class Settings and add BPI_Interact under Implemented Interfaces. Then add Event Interact to the graph and make it call ToggleLight.

Make a Blueprint named BP_Door with two Static Mesh components named Frame and Door. Add a custom event named OpenDoor that uses a Timeline named TM_Door, with an Alpha value that goes from 0 to 1. Use a Lerp node to turn the door Yaw to 90.
Add BPI_Interact to BP_Door in the same way. Implement Event Interact there and make it call OpenDoor.
In ThirdPersonCharacter, add a Sphere Collision component with Radius 200. On its begin overlap event, call Interact (Message) and connect Other Actor to the Target pin.
Place BP_Lamp, BP_Door and a plain cube in the level. Press Play and walk near all three. Nothing should happen at the plain cube, because it does not use the interface.
PQ34.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Class Settings panel of one actor that shows BPI_Interact under Implemented Interfaces, and a screenshot in Play mode with the door open and the lamp toggled.

PQ35.brief: An Event Dispatcher is a way for one Actor to announce that something happened, without knowing who is listening. Other Actors bind to the dispatcher, which means they sign up to be told, and they all react when it is called. This keeps Actors independent: the boss does not need to know about the doors. In this quest one trigger box announces that a boss died, and a door and several explosions react at the same time.
checklist: Make a Blueprint named BP_BossDied with a Box Collision component. Set its scale to 4, 4, 2 and turn off Hidden in Game so you can see the box while you play. Add an Event Dispatcher named OnBossDied.
On the OnComponentBeginOverlap event of the box, add the Call OnBossDied node. Place BP_BossDied in the level.
Make a Blueprint named BP_BossDoor with a Frame mesh and a Door mesh. Add a custom event named OpenDoor that uses a Timeline named TM_Door to rotate the door to Yaw 90.

In BP_BossDoor, add an Instance Editable variable named BossDiedReference with the type BP_BossDied Object Reference. On BeginPlay, use Bind Event to OnBossDied and connect a custom event named BossDied that calls OpenDoor.
Make a copy of Blueprint_Effect_Explosion. Turn off Auto Activate on both of its components. On BeginPlay, use Assign OnBossDied, and make the new event Activate both components.
Place the door and 3 explosions in the level. On each one, set BossDiedReference to the BP_BossDied you placed. Press Play and walk into the box.
Extra: on one explosion, add an Unbind All Events node after it fires. Test that this explosion does not fire a second time.
PQ35.done_when: Send a screenshot of the BP_BossDoor graph that shows Bind Event to OnBossDied, and a screenshot in Play mode with the door open and the explosions active at the same time.

PQ36.brief: A Blueprint Function Library is an asset that holds helper functions that any Blueprint in your project can call. It is the right place for small tools, such as a piece of math, that do not belong to one Actor. Without it, people copy the same nodes into many Blueprints. In this quest you make a library with two functions and call them from an Actor.
checklist: In the Content Browser, create a new asset by choosing Blueprints, then Blueprint Function Library. Name it BFL_Utils.
Add a function named DistanceXY with two Vector inputs and one Float output. Mark it as Pure, which means it only returns a value and changes nothing. Build the math from the two inputs.
Add a second function named PrintWithPrefix with a String input. Leave it impure (do not check Pure). Inside, it calls Print String with a prefix in front of the text.
In any Actor Blueprint, call both functions on Event Tick and on BeginPlay. Notice that the pure function has no exec pins, the white pins that set the order of execution.
Set a Category on both functions. Then right-click in a graph and check that the functions appear under that category in the menu.
Change the number of inputs on DistanceXY and look at the node where you call it. Click Compile and see the warning go away.
PQ36.done_when: Send a screenshot of BFL_Utils with the two functions, and a screenshot of a graph that calls both and shows the pure node without exec pins.

PQ37.brief: A macro is a small group of nodes that you save under one name and reuse, like a function. Unlike a function, a macro can have more than one output exec pin, and it can hold nodes that wait, such as Delay. A Blueprint Macro Library is an asset that stores macros so that many Blueprints can use them. In this quest you make a library with two macros and use them in an Actor.
checklist: In the Content Browser, create a new asset by choosing Blueprints, then Blueprint Macro Library. Pick Actor as the Parent Class and name the library BML_Flow.

Add a macro named CheckScore. Give it an Integer input named Score, an input exec pin named Test, and two output exec pins named Win and Lose. Inside the macro, compare Score to 10 to decide which output runs.
Add a macro named WaitThenPrint with a String input and a Delay node inside. Notice that a Delay is allowed in a macro.
Select each macro and, in the Details panel, set an Instance Color and a Category for it.
In an Actor Blueprint, use CheckScore on BeginPlay and connect one Print String to Win and another to Lose. Then use WaitThenPrint.
Change something in the macro in the library. Then compile the Actor Blueprint and confirm that the change appears there.
PQ37.done_when: Send a screenshot of BML_Flow that shows CheckScore with its two output exec pins, and a screenshot of an Actor graph that uses both macros.

PQ38.brief: A Blueprint Actor has two places where setup logic can run. The Construction Script runs in the editor each time the Actor is placed or changed, so you see its result before you press Play. Event BeginPlay runs only when the game starts or when the Actor is spawned during play. Putting logic in the wrong one causes strange bugs. In this quest you use both and see when each one runs.
checklist: Make a Blueprint named BP_Post with a Static Mesh. Add an Integer variable named Count with a default of 3, and make it Instance Editable so you can change it on each placed copy.
In the Construction Script, add a loop that runs Count times. In each pass, use Add Static Mesh Component, and place the meshes 150 units apart.
Place BP_Post in the level. Change Count in the Details panel and watch the meshes update in the editor, before you press Play.
Add Event BeginPlay and make it print Hello. Add Event End Play and make it print the End Play Reason. Press Play and then stop.
Add an Instance Editable Linear Color variable and turn on Expose on Spawn for it. In the Level Blueprint, use Spawn Actor from Class with BP_Post and set the color on the spawn node.
Write down which script ran in the editor and which one ran only in Play.
PQ38.done_when: Send a screenshot of the editor viewport that shows BP_Post rebuilt after you changed Count (without pressing Play), and a screenshot of the Output Log that shows the BeginPlay and End Play messages.

PQ39.brief: Every Actor goes through the same steps in its life: it is constructed, then BeginPlay runs, and when it is removed EndPlay runs. If you know this order, you can explain most bugs where a value is still empty when you try to use it. In this quest you build a small test Actor that prints a message at each step, and you read the order in the Output Log.
checklist: Make a Blueprint Actor named BP_LifeProbe with a Static Mesh that is a cube. On Event BeginPlay, add a Print String that prints the actor name plus 'BeginPlay'.
Add Event End Play. Make it print the actor name plus 'EndPlay' and also the End Play Reason.
In the Construction Script, add a Print String that prints 'Construct'. Drag BP_LifeProbe into the level and watch the message appear before you press Play.

In the Level Blueprint, add an event for key 1 that uses Spawn Actor from Class to spawn BP_LifeProbe at the player location. Add an event for key 2 that calls Destroy Actor on the last probe you spawned.
Press Play. Press 1 and then 2. Read the Output Log and note the order of the messages: Construct, BeginPlay, EndPlay.
Spawn a probe and stop Play In Editor (PIE) while the probe is still alive. Check the log: End Play fires again, and this time the reason is End Play in Editor.
PQ39.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Output Log that shows the Construct, BeginPlay and EndPlay messages in order for one spawned probe, and a second EndPlay line with the End Play in Editor reason.

PQ40.brief: An Actor is built from components, which are parts such as a mesh, a light or a collision box. The components form a tree: when one component is the child of another, it moves together with its parent. Every Actor you will ever make is a tree like this, so you need to be able to read and build it. In this quest you build a lantern from several components and test how the parent and child links behave.
checklist: Make a Blueprint Actor named BP_Lantern and keep the default Scene root. Add a Static Mesh Component for the pole, a second Static Mesh for the lamp head, and a Point Light.
In the Components window, drag the lamp head onto the pole so that it becomes a child of the pole. Then drag the Point Light onto the lamp head.
Select the pole and move it in the viewport. Confirm that the head and the light move with it. Then move only the head and confirm that only the light follows.
Select each component, press F2, and rename them to Pole, Head and Light. Check the new names in the My Blueprint panel.
Add a Rotating Movement Component. Press Play and see the lantern spin. Notice that this component has no transform in the viewport, which means it has no position of its own.
Add a Box Component named Trigger. In the Details panel, click Add Event and pick On Component Begin Overlap. Make it print a string when the player walks into the box.
PQ40.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Components window of BP_Lantern that shows the hierarchy with Pole, then Head, then Light, plus the Rotating Movement and Trigger components. Also send a screenshot in Play mode with the overlap message on screen.

PQ41.brief: Attaching means making one Actor follow another, for example an item that follows the hand of a character. Detaching lets it go again. Picking up items, holding tools and mounting turrets all work this way. The attach and detach nodes have rules that decide if the object jumps to the new parent or keeps its place in the world. In this quest you attach a ball to the hand of the character with one key and drop it with another.
checklist: Make a Blueprint named BP_Ball with a Static Mesh sphere as its root, and set the scale to 0.3. Set its Mobility to Movable so that it can move during play.
Open the Third Person character (BP_ThirdPersonCharacter). Open its Skeletal Mesh in the Skeleton editor and note the name of a socket or bone on the right hand (for example hand_r).

In the character, add an event for the E key. Call Get All Actors Of Class with BP_Ball and take index 0 from the result. Then call Attach Actor To Component with Parent set to the character Mesh and Socket Name set to the hand bone. Set Location Rule and Rotation Rule to Snap to Target.
Add an event for the Q key. Call Detach From Actor on the same ball, with Location Rule set to Keep World.
Press Play. Walk near the ball, press E, then run around and watch the ball follow the hand. Press Q and confirm that the ball stays where you dropped it.
Change the Location Rule of the attach node to Keep World and test again. Note what is different.
PQ41.done_when: Send two screenshots taken in Play mode: one with the ball attached to the character's hand while moving, and one with the ball left in the world after the detach. Also include the Blueprint graph with the Attach and Detach nodes.

PQ42.brief: A tag is a short name that you can add to an Actor or to a component, such as Breakable. Your Blueprints can then find everything that has that tag. Tags let a designer mark things in the level without making a new Blueprint class for them. In this quest you tag some cubes, find them from a Blueprint, and also find one component by its tag.
checklist: Place six cubes in a test level and select three of them. In the Details panel, find the Tags property in the Actor section and add the tag Breakable to each of the three.
Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_TagScanner. On BeginPlay, call Get All Actors with Tag with Tag set to Breakable. Print the length of the array it returns. You should see 3.
Loop through the array. For each actor, call Actor Has Tag with Breakable and print the actor name. Then try the tag Wall and see that it returns false.

Make a Blueprint named BP_Crate with two Static Mesh Components. Select one component and add the component tag Lid in the Tags property of its Details panel. In BeginPlay, call Find Component by Tag with the class Static Mesh Component and the tag Lid, and set the material of the result to something red.
Change one call in the scanner to Get All Actors Of Class with Tag, with the class Static Mesh Actor and the tag Breakable. Compare the count with the one from before.
Write two lines for your proof: one that says when a tag is easier than a new Blueprint class, and one that says why the tag search should not run every frame.
PQ42.done_when: Send a screenshot in Play mode with the printed count and names, a screenshot of the Tags array of one cube in the Details panel, and your two lines about tags compared with classes and about the cost of the search.
